items.q: My cousin (A) has moved to Da Nang two years ago, and she (B) still sends us photos of the beach (C) whenever the weather (D) is nice.
items.explanation: A finished action with a definite past time (two years ago) takes the past simple, not the present perfect.

items.q: Before the experiment, the teacher (A) reminded us that each of the coloured liquids (B) were dangerous (C) if it touched (D) our skin.
items.explanation: Each of + plural noun is a singular subject, so the verb must be singular (was); the pronoun it later in the sentence confirms this.

items.q: During the Tet holiday, my brother (A) worked as a guide for (B) a group of climbers who wanted to reach (C) the top of the Mount Fansipan (D) before dawn.
options: the top of the Mount Fansipan
items.explanation: The names of individual mountains (Mount Fansipan, Mount Everest) take no article; only mountain ranges do (the Alps).

items.q: The documentary about penguins (A) was so interesting that my little sister (B) insisted on watching it again (C) as soon as we (D) arrived at home.
items.explanation: Home behaves like an adverb after verbs of movement: we arrive home, go home, get home, with no preposition.

items.q: The (A) succeed of the school football team (B) depends largely on (C) how well the players (D) communicate with one another during the match.
items.explanation: After the and before of a noun is needed, so the verb succeed must become the noun success.

items.q: Because Lan and I (A) had finished the science project (B) by ourself, the teacher praised us (C) in front of (D) the whole class.
items.explanation: The reflexive pronoun for we is the plural form ourselves; ourself is not a standard form.

items.q: Although the new library is (A) much bigger than the old one, most students (B) still think the reading room (C) is more quieter in (D) the old building.
items.explanation: A short adjective forms its comparative with -er alone; more and -er are never used together.

items.q: Scientists say that (A) if the ice at the poles (B) continues to melt at this speed, many coastal cities (C) will face serious floods (D) unless they will build higher walls.
items.explanation: In a first conditional the if/unless clause takes the present simple; will belongs only in the main clause.

items.q: Yesterday the coach (A) said us that the final match (B) would be postponed (C) until the pitch (D) had dried out.
items.explanation: Tell takes a direct object (told us that...), whereas say needs to before the person (said to us).

items.q: Last month our class visited a factory (A) on the outskirts of the city (B) which the workers make bicycles (C) that are sold (D) all over Asia.
items.explanation: The clause already has its own subject and object (the workers make bicycles), so a relative adverb of place, where, is needed rather than the pronoun which.

items.q: My father (A) usually reads the newspaper (B) at breakfast, but this morning he (C) asked me what time was the bus (D) leaving for the airport.
options: asked me what time was the bus
items.correction: asked me what time the bus was
items.explanation: In an indirect question the subject comes before the verb (what time the bus was), with no inversion.

items.q: After school, my sister (A) usually helps my mother (B) prepare dinner while I (C) walk the dog and (D) make the washing-up.
items.explanation: Household chores collocate with do: do the washing-up, do the cooking, do the housework.

items.q: (A) A few of the furniture in the hall (B) was damaged when the roof (C) leaked during the heavy storm (D) last Tuesday night.
items.explanation: Furniture is uncountable, so it cannot follow a few; use some or a little instead.

items.q: My uncle (A) still cycles to work every day (B) despite he is nearly seventy and (C) the road is (D) quite hilly.
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or -ing form; a full clause with subject and verb needs although or even though.

items.q: By the time the fire engine (A) arrived at the market, the shopkeepers (B) had already carried most of their goods outside and (C) are waiting (D) on the pavement.
items.explanation: The whole sentence describes a past scene (arrived, had carried), so the ongoing action must be in the past continuous, not the present.

items.q: The number of students (A) who bring their own lunch (B) to school (C) has increased since the canteen prices (D) was raised in March.
items.explanation: The subject of the final clause is the plural noun prices, so the passive verb must be plural: were raised.

items.q: (A) The honesty is the quality my grandmother (B) valued most, and she (C) never forgave anyone who (D) told her a lie.
items.explanation: An abstract noun used in a general sense (honesty, freedom, happiness) takes no article.

items.q: The astronomy club meets (A) on the roof of the science building (B) in Friday evenings, when the sky (C) is usually clear enough (D) to see Jupiter.
items.explanation: We say in the evening, but once a day is named the preposition becomes on: on Friday evenings, on Monday morning.

items.q: The bus driver (A) drove very (B) carefully along the mountain road, but the passengers were still (C) frighten by the (D) sharp bends.
items.explanation: To describe how people feel we need the -ed adjective (frightened), not the bare verb frighten.

items.q: The old clock in the hall (A) stopped working last week, so my father (B) took it to a repair shop (C) whose owner promised to fix (D) them by Friday.
items.explanation: The pronoun refers back to the singular clock, so it must be it, matching the earlier took it.

items.q: Mai is (A) the most tall girl in her class, (B) which is why the coach (C) asked her to try out for the (D) volleyball team.
items.explanation: One-syllable adjectives form the superlative with -est; most is used only with longer adjectives.

items.q: If I (A) had a bigger garden, I (B) will grow my own vegetables (C) instead of buying them (D) from the supermarket every week.
items.explanation: The past simple in the if clause signals a second conditional, whose main clause takes would + verb.

items.q: The weather forecaster (A) warned viewers last night that a typhoon (B) was heading towards the coast and (C) will reach land (D) within two days.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb (warned) the tenses shift back, so will becomes would to match was heading.

items.q: Nobody in my family (A) has ever visited the island off the northern coast, (B) although we have (C) often admired the photos (D) which my aunt took them there.
options: which my aunt took them there
items.explanation: The relative pronoun which already acts as the object of took, so the extra object pronoun them must be removed.

items.q: My brother (A) enjoys very much the science programme (B) that is shown (C) on television (D) every Sunday evening.
options: enjoys very much the science programme
items.correction: enjoys the science programme very much
items.explanation: An adverb of degree such as very much cannot separate a verb from its object; it goes after the object.

items.q: Our science teacher (A) encouraged us to (B) make more attention (C) to the safety rules (D) before lighting the burner.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is pay attention to; make attention does not exist in English.

items.q: There (A) were so many people at the night market (B) that we could hardly move, and there (C) wasn't many room to sit down (D) and eat.
items.explanation: Room meaning space is uncountable, so it takes much, not many; the singular wasn't is the clue.

items.q: After the concert (A) finished at ten, we (B) decided to walk (C) all the way home (D) because of the buses were full.
options: because of the buses were full
items.explanation: Because of is followed by a noun phrase; a clause with its own verb (the buses were full) needs the conjunction because.

items.q: (A) Ten kilometres are a long way to walk (B) in this heat, so (C) we should leave (D) before sunrise.
items.explanation: A distance, sum of money or period of time is treated as a single amount and takes a singular verb: ten kilometres is a long way.

items.q: Don't worry, I (A) will send you the photos (B) as soon as I will get home (C) from the trip (D) this evening.
options: as soon as I will get home
items.correction: as soon as I get home
items.explanation: After time conjunctions like as soon as, when and until, the present simple is used for future time, never will.

items.q: My uncle, (A) who lives in Can Tho, is (B) a farmer, but his daughter is (C) engineer at (D) a large company in the city.
items.explanation: A singular countable noun naming someone's job needs an article: a farmer, an engineer.

items.q: The picnic (A) that our class has planned for Saturday (B) will take place at the lake, but (C) whether we swim or not (D) depends of the weather.
items.explanation: The verb depend is always followed by the preposition on, never of.

items.q: (A) Unfortunate, the school concert (B) had to be cancelled because (C) the singer had lost her voice (D) the day before.
items.explanation: A comment on the whole sentence is made with a sentence adverb ending in -ly, not with the adjective.

items.q: The twins look (A) so alike that even their teacher (B) sometimes confuses one with other, (C) especially when they wear (D) the same uniform.
items.correction: sometimes confuses one with the other
items.explanation: When there are exactly two, the second one is the other; other alone cannot stand as a pronoun.

items.q: The train journey to Hue (A) takes about twelve hours, (B) which is (C) far longer as the flight, (D) but the views are wonderful.
items.explanation: A comparative adjective (longer) is followed by than; as belongs only to the pattern as ... as.

items.q: Tuan (A) failed his driving test (B) last month, and his father (C) said he would have passed (D) if he would have practised more.
options: if he would have practised more
items.explanation: A third conditional puts the past perfect in the if clause; would have is used only in the main clause.

items.q: Last week the principal (A) announced that the school would close tomorrow (B) because of the flood, (C) so most students (D) stayed at home.
options: announced that the school would close tomorrow
items.correction: announced that the school would close the next day
items.explanation: When speech is reported from a past time (last week), time words shift too: tomorrow becomes the next day or the following day.

items.q: Every morning my grandfather (A) gets up at five, (B) makes a short walk around the lake and (C) then has (D) a bowl of pho.
items.explanation: English says go for a walk or take a walk; make a walk is not a collocation.

items.q: Although we (A) had arrived at the airport early, my mother worried that there (B) were (C) too little seats left near the gate (D) for the whole family.
items.explanation: Seats is a plural countable noun, so it takes few; little is used only with uncountable nouns.

items.q: The recipe (A) says you should (B) let the dough rest (C) for an hour, (D) otherwise the bread will not raise properly.
options: otherwise the bread will not raise properly
items.correction: otherwise the bread will not rise properly
items.explanation: Rise is intransitive (something rises by itself), while raise needs an object (you raise something); bread rises.
